title: Photoelectric Effect
short_intro: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metallic surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency falls upon it. It provides definitive proof of the particle nature of light through Einstein's photon hypothesis.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition, threshold frequency, work function, Einstein's photoelectric equation, and dependence of stopping potential on frequency and intensity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed analysis of stopping potential vs. frequency graphs, determination of Planck's constant, particle nature of photons, momentum of photons, and relativistic photoelectric considerations.

prerequisites: Work function and binding energy of electrons in metals

concept_notes.heading: Basic Phenomenon and Experimental Observations
bullets: Photoelectric emission is an instantaneous process with no measurable time lag between light incidence and electron ejection.
Emission occurs only if the incident frequency exceeds a specific minimum frequency called the threshold frequency (ν<sub>0</sub>).
The maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is independent of the intensity of incident light and depends solely on its frequency.

concept_notes.heading: Einstein's Explanation and Photon Hypothesis
bullets: Light propagates in discrete packets of energy called photons, each having energy E = hν.
A single photon transfers its entire energy to a single electron in an elastic-like collision at the surface.
The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron is governed by the conservation of energy: K<sub>max</sub> = hν - φ, where φ is the work function.

concept_notes.heading: Role of Intensity and Frequency
bullets: Increasing the intensity of incident light (at a constant frequency) increases the number of incident photons per second, thereby increasing the photoelectric current.
Increasing the frequency of incident light increases the energy of individual photons, resulting in higher maximum kinetic energy and greater stopping potential.
Below the threshold frequency, no photoelectrons are emitted regardless of how high the incident light intensity is.

concept_notes.heading: Stopping Potential Concept
bullets: Stopping potential (V<sub>s</sub>) is the minimum negative potential applied to the anode that reduces the photoelectric current to zero.
It provides a direct measure of the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons via the relation e V<sub>s</sub> = K<sub>max</sub>.
The slope of the stopping potential versus frequency graph gives the universal constant ratio h/e.

derivations.title: Derivation of Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and Stopping Potential
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic light of frequency ν incident on a clean metal surface with work function φ
steps: Apply conservation of energy to the interaction between a single photon and an electron: Energy of photon = Work function + Maximum kinetic energy of emitted electron.
Substitute the expressions: h\nu = \phi + K_{max}, where \phi = h\nu_{0} (ν<sub>0</sub> is threshold frequency).
Express maximum kinetic energy in terms of stopping potential V<sub>s</sub>: K_{max} = e V_{s}.
Combine the relations to obtain the final voltage-frequency equation: e V_{s} = h\nu - h\nu_{0}.

derivations.title: Derivation of Photon Momentum and Radiation Pressure
derivations.conditions: Photons considered as relativistic particles with zero rest mass
steps: Use the energy-momentum relation for a particle with zero rest mass: E = pc, where p is momentum and c is the speed of light.
Substitute the photon energy E = h\nu: pc = h\nu.
Express momentum in terms of wavelength λ using c = νλ: p = \frac{h\nu}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda}.
For complete absorption at a surface, force F = \frac{dn}{dt} p, where \frac{dn}{dt} is the number of photons striking per second.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stopping Potential vs. Frequency Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of stopping potential (V<sub>s</sub>) on the y-axis against frequency (ν) on the x-axis, intersecting the x-axis at ν<sub>0</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The intercept on the frequency axis gives the threshold frequency ν<sub>0</sub>. The slope of the line is equal to h/e, independent of the metal used.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used to calculate Planck's constant experimentally and to determine work function.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Photoelectric Current vs. Anode Potential
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves showing saturation current at positive potentials and dropping to zero at a negative stopping potential (-V<sub>s</sub>) for different light intensities at constant frequency.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Saturation current is directly proportional to intensity, but the stopping potential remains identical for all curves sharing the same frequency.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tests understanding of the independence of maximum kinetic energy from light intensity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lenard's Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An evacuated quartz bulb containing an emitter plate (C) and a collector plate (A), connected to a variable voltage source, reversing switch, and sensitive microammeter.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the control of electron flow using retarding and accelerating potentials under monochromatic illumination.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on experimental design, vacuum requirements, and role of quartz windows.

solved_numericals.question: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. Calculate its threshold wavelength. (Take hc = 12400 eV Å)
solution_steps: Identify given values: φ = 2.0 eV, hc = 12400 eV Å.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 4000 Å falls on a photosensitive metal with work function 2.5 eV. Find the maximum velocity of the emitted photoelectrons. (Mass of electron m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}, h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}, c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}, 1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J})
solution_steps: Calculate energy of incident photon in Joules: E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{4000 \times 10^{-10}} = 4.9725 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}.
Convert work function to Joules: \phi = 2.5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.0 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}.
Calculate maximum kinetic energy: K_{max} = E - \phi = 4.9725 \times 10^{-19} - 4.0 \times 10^{-19} = 0.9725 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}.

solved_numericals.question: When monochromatic light of frequency 1.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz} is incident on a metallic plate, the stopping potential is found to be 2.0 V. When the frequency is changed to 2.0 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}, the stopping potential becomes 4.0 V. Calculate the value of Planck's constant from these data, given the electronic charge e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}.
solution_steps: Write the stopping potential equations for both frequencies: e V_{s1} = h\nu_{1} - \phi and e V_{s2} = h\nu_{2} - \phi.
Subtract the first equation from the second: e(V_{s2} - V_{s1}) = h(\nu_{2} - \nu_{1}).
Solve for h: h = \frac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{0.5 \times 10^{15}} = 6.4 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Single-photon absorption by a single electron without multiple scattering events inside the metal. Limitation: High-intensity laser beams can induce multi-photon photoelectric emission.

Assumption: Zero rest mass approximation for photons interacting with non-relativistic electrons. Limitation: At extremely high gamma-ray energies, pair production competes with photoelectric emission.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Increasing the intensity of incident light increases the kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons.
common_misconceptions.correct: Increasing light intensity increases the number of emitted photoelectrons (current), but their maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: Intensity governs the photon flux density, whereas photon frequency determines individual photon energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Photoelectric emission takes time to accumulate sufficient energy if the light is very dim.
common_misconceptions.correct: Photoelectric emission is instantaneous once the threshold frequency condition is met.
common_misconceptions.why: Energy transfer happens via localized photon packets instantaneously, not via continuous classical wave energy accumulation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Any frequency of light can cause photoelectric emission if the exposure time is long enough.
common_misconceptions.correct: Light with frequency below the threshold frequency produces no photoelectrons, regardless of duration or intensity.
common_misconceptions.why: A single photon must carry energy greater than or equal to the work function to eject an electron.

quick_revision: Photoelectric emission proves the quantum particle nature of light.
Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency required for electron emission.
Stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons.
Einstein's photoelectric equation is based on conservation of energy in photon-electron collisions.
